# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

## Interpretation of Results {#sec-discussion-interpretation}

Our first finding concerns the wages of employees. We find that employees of small single-site workplaces earn about 11 per cent less than similar employees of large workplaces in the same industry and year. This wage penalty becomes much smaller, falling to under 2 per cent, in industries where a third of business owners are non-English-speaking migrants who speak English well. However, the penalty does not become smaller in industries with more owners who have limited English. When we replace the origin-specific owner densities with the share of all migrant owners and the share of owners with limited English, only the share of all migrant owners matters. That is, the smaller wage penalty is linked to migrant ownership in general and not to owners' language barriers. This is not what Result 3 of our framework predicts.

The idea behind the framework is still reasonable. English proficiency is valuable for earnings in Australia [@budria_education_2021], migrants from non-English-speaking countries take a long time to catch up with the wages of the native-born [@breunig_immigrant_2013], and migrant owners can come to depend on their local employees in practice [@cooke_2022]. However, there are very few migrant owners with limited English in HILDA, only 47 in waves 1 to 21. As a result, the owner density for this group is zero for 64 per cent of the employees in our sample. Our data therefore cannot confirm or rule out a moderate effect of these owners on wages.

The pay structure of industries offers another explanation for the wage results. Wages differ widely across firm sizes and industries [@brown_employer_1989]. In Australia, the share of employees paid exactly the award wage is highest in accommodation and food services [@australianbureauofstatistics_guide_2019], which is also the lowest-paying industry [@australianbureauofstatistics_employee_2026] and an industry in which migrants make up around a third of owners. When most employees are paid the award wage, small and large firms pay similar wages regardless of who owns them. In such industries, we would expect the wage penalty for small workplaces to be small even without any effect of migrant ownership. Our industry-by-year fixed effects remove differences in average wages between industries, but they do not remove differences in the size of the small-workplace penalty. Our robustness check with chain workplaces shows that this matters. Migrants rarely own small sites of chains, yet these workplaces also pay relatively more in industries with many English-proficient MNES owners, by about half as much as small independent workplaces. Ethnic networks offer a further explanation, since working with people from the same background can raise earnings [@edin_ethnic_2003], although @xie_ethnic_2011 do not find this in every setting.

Our wage results also add to the literature on the pay of migrant workers. Previous studies show that the wage gap between immigrants and the native-born arises mainly because immigrants work in lower-paying jobs and firms, and not because they are paid less for the same job [@han_wage_2024; @hermansen_immigrantnative_2025]. We find that the industries in which migrants own businesses also have smaller pay differences between workplace types. This pattern could reflect how wages are set in these industries, ethnic networks or bargaining, but it does not point specifically to owners with language barriers.

The bargaining power of employees also depends on their own options outside the job. @berg_wage_2017 show that employers in Australia often underpay migrant workers who depend on their visas, and that these employers are often from the same community as the workers. This suggests that bargaining power can only shift towards employees who have good alternatives, such as the skilled, English-proficient employee in our framework. Our wage measure includes all employees of small single-site workplaces. Higher pay for employees with good alternatives could therefore exist alongside the underpayment of more vulnerable employees.

One wage result was unexpected. We find that the wage penalty for small workplaces becomes larger in industries with more MES owners, even though these owners face no language barrier. This result most likely reflects the kinds of industries and businesses that MES owners run. It also means that MES owners are a weaker point of comparison than we expected.

Our second finding is that owning a business with employees brings higher income but also higher risk, and that this is true in every origin group. Native-born small employers earn about \$12,700 a year more than native-born employees of small workplaces. However, their income changes by 27 percentage points more from year to year, and they are 15 percentage points more likely to experience a fall in income of a quarter or more. Small employers from every migrant group show the same pattern when compared with employees of their own origin. That is, owners are compensated for the extra risk they bear. Own-account workers, in contrast, earn less than employees. These results are consistent with evidence from the United States that owners of incorporated businesses earn more than employees, while owners of small unincorporated businesses earn much less [@levine_smart_2017]. They also help explain why studies that group all the self-employed together find that self-employment does not pay [@hamilton_does_2000]. Our results also support the view that owners bear income risk because they receive what is left after all costs are paid [@bhandari_nature_2026; @audoly_self-employment_2025]. Our comparison of hourly income shows that much of the extra annual income of owners comes from working longer hours. In low-margin industries such as accommodation and food services, owners with employees earn less per hour than employees of small independent workplaces.

Our test of power reversal on the owner side does not give a clear answer. If power reversal holds, small employers with limited English should earn less and face more risk than native-born small employers, when each is compared with employees of their own origin. We find that the risk results point in this direction. The income of these owners is 12 percentage points more volatile, and their chance of a large fall is 4 percentage points higher, than the native-born comparison suggests. However, their income result points in the opposite direction, and none of these differences is statistically significant. Our unrestricted sample contains only 21 small employers with limited English. With so few owners, our tests could only reliably detect differences of about \$30,000 a year in income and 34 percentage points in volatility. We therefore cannot conclude that these owners do as well as native-born owners. We can only conclude that our data are not precise enough to tell.

Our results for own-account workers are consistent with earlier Australian evidence. @le_self-employment_1999 found that immigrants in Australia earned less in self-employment than the native-born. In our data, own-account workers with limited English also earn less, but much of this gap already exists among employees with limited English. This is consistent with evidence that immigrants who become self-employed were already underpaid as employees [@villarreal_role_2026], and that English proficiency affects the earnings of self-employed immigrants [@davila_english-language_2004].

We also find that the income of own-account workers with limited English appears less volatile than the native-born comparison suggests. This result appears only in the restricted sample, which includes only people who stay in the same status for two years in a row. When we also include people who have just become own-account workers, the difference becomes smaller and is no longer significant. We think this reflects which businesses survive. Businesses run by immigrants have a high risk of failure [@brzozowski_impact_2019], so the own-account workers with limited English who stay in that status for two years are likely to be those with stable businesses. The way people report income in surveys may also play a role, since the self-employed tend to under-report their income [@hurst_are_2014], and surveys measure immigrant self-employment differently for different origin groups [@tamborini_research_2025].

Our third finding is that people enter business ownership from weak positions in the labour market. We find that being unemployed, being out of the labour force, earning a low wage and facing financial difficulty all make entry into ownership more likely. This is consistent with research that identifies necessity entrepreneurship by people's work status before they start a business [@fairlie_2020]. For the native-born, being unemployed raises the odds of entering ownership by a factor of 1.9. For migrants with limited English, it raises the odds by a factor of 7.9, which is more than four times the effect for the native-born. However, this result is based on only five migrants with limited English who entered ownership after being unemployed. The difference is also not significant when we measure it as a change in probability instead of a change in odds. This is because so few migrants with limited English enter ownership from stable employment, so a large change in their odds is only a small change in their probability of entry [@ai_interaction_2003].

The timing of entry supports this interpretation. For the native-born, only unemployment in the year just before entry predicts entry. This could mean that losing a job pushes people into ownership, but it could also mean that people leave their jobs to prepare for a business they had already planned. We cannot tell these two apart for the native-born. For migrants with limited English, unemployment two years before entry predicts entry just as strongly, and the result remains when we compare each person with themselves at other times. That is, these migrants enter ownership after a long period without good alternatives, not after a single short spell of unemployment. This pattern is difficult to explain by planning ahead, and it matches the type of necessity entry that our framework assumes.

Two further results add to this picture. First, among people in stable and reasonably paid jobs, migrants with limited English are less likely to enter ownership than the native-born, with 0.59 times the odds. The low income and limited savings that push people towards ownership may also make it harder for them to start a business when they are not pushed. Second, people with more education are more likely to enter ownership. This suggests that people are both pushed into ownership by poor alternatives and pulled into it by good opportunities [@fairlie_2020].

Some explanations for migrant self-employment are not included in our models. Discrimination in paid employment can push minorities into self-employment, while opportunities within their own communities can pull them in [@clark_ethnicity_1998]. Immigrant self-employment also rises with time spent in the host country [@borjas_self-employment_1986], and in Australia it is more common in communities that share a language [@le_determinants_2000]. Studies also point to the role of overseas qualifications that are not recognised and of visa conditions. HILDA does not record this information for most respondents, so we cannot examine these explanations.

Overall, our three analyses give a mixed picture of the framework. The wage results show that migrant ownership is linked to the pay of employees in small workplaces, but not through owners' language barriers. The income results cannot confirm or rule out the prediction that owners with limited English earn less or bear more risk. The entry results support the framework's assumption that these owners have few alternatives and find it costly to leave their business. In the framework, it is this cost of leaving, $K$, that gives workers more bargaining power. Our data therefore support the first step of the mechanism, but we cannot observe the second step. The clearest disadvantage of migrants with limited English appears at the point when they enter business ownership.

## Limitations and Future Research {#sec-discussion-limitations}

Our analysis has several limitations. We discuss each one in turn, together with the research that could address it.

First, we do not observe bargaining, compliance decisions or the delegation of tasks within firms, and HILDA does not link workers to their employers. We therefore test the predictions of power reversal instead of observing the mechanism directly. We also measure each worker's exposure to migrant ownership by the mix of owners in their industry and year. This means that every small single-site workplace in the same industry and year receives the same exposure, whether or not a migrant owns it. Our wage results therefore show the link between migrant ownership and pay at the industry level, and not the effect of working for a migrant owner. Our robustness check with chain workplaces shows that part of this link reflects the pay structure of industries. Future research could use linked employer–employee data, such as administrative data that link Australian tax records to businesses, to compare the wages of workers in migrant-owned and native-owned firms in the same industry. Future studies could also allow the small-workplace penalty to differ by industry, or measure the density of migrant workers instead of migrant owners, to separate the effect of ownership from the pay structure of industries and ethnic networks. Surveys that ask owners how they manage compliance, and how much they rely on employees and advisers for regulatory knowledge, would test the information gap in our framework directly.

Second, our estimates show associations, not causal effects. We use a rich set of controls and fixed effects instead of individual fixed effects. Individual fixed effects would remove origin and English proficiency, which do not change over time, and would estimate the interactions only from the few people who change status. Our wage results could therefore reflect migrant owners choosing to start businesses in industries where small workplaces already pay relatively well. If so, our results would overstate any effect of migrant ownership. Future research could use changes in the number of migrant business owners that are unrelated to local wages, such as changes to business and skilled visa programs, to estimate causal effects.

Third, our sample of migrants with limited English is small. HILDA records only 47 owners with limited English in waves 1 to 21, and our owner income analysis includes only 21 small employers with limited English. HILDA also under-represents recent immigrants, who are the most likely to have limited English [@watson_finding_2021; @watson_comparison_2026]. These small numbers affect all three analyses. The smallest differences that we can detect for owners with limited English are large. The owner density for this group changes sign depending on the survey weight we use to construct it. The larger push into ownership for migrants with limited English is based on only five entries. When an owner density rests on few owners, it also contains measurement error, which pulls its estimated effect on wages towards zero. We therefore treat many of the results for this group as uninformative, and not as evidence of no effect. Administrative data that cover all migrant business owners, or surveys that include more recent migrants with limited English, would allow future research to test our predictions for the group that the framework focuses on.

Fourth, our owner densities vary across only 19 industries and change slowly over time within each industry. Our wage results therefore rely on a small number of independent comparisons. When we define industries more narrowly, the results become weaker, partly because each narrower industry contains even fewer owners. Future studies could measure owner density at a more detailed level, such as by industry and region, although this would require larger samples of owners than HILDA provides.

Fifth, income in HILDA is reported by respondents and refers to the financial year before the interview. For people who changed status between interviews, income therefore partly reflects their previous status. We address this by comparing the restricted and unrestricted samples. The self-employed also tend to under-report their income in household surveys [@hurst_are_2014]. In addition, both of our samples classify people by their status in the later year. Neither sample therefore shows what happens to the income of owners whose business closes, and owners who leave the survey drop out of both samples. Tax records that follow owners through the start and closure of their businesses would allow future research to measure the full range of returns to ownership, including the losses from failed businesses.

Sixth, for the native-born, our entry analysis cannot separate entry that is pushed by job loss from entry that people plan in advance, since their push comes only from the year just before entry. Our two methods that compare each person with themselves at other times also disagree. They give different answers on whether low wages, and the larger push from unemployment for migrants with limited English, work within the same person. Both methods assume that starting a business does not affect a person's later employment status. This assumption is doubtful, since owners who close their business return to the sample with an employment history shaped by their business. Future research could use methods that allow for this feedback, together with a longer panel of migrants with limited English.

Future research could also extend our analysis of entry in two ways. First, our measure of entry groups together very different types of business, incorporated and unincorporated, with and without employees. People who start these businesses differ, and so do their reasons for starting them. In the United States, the incorporated self-employed earn more than similar salaried workers and have stronger cognitive skills, while the unincorporated self-employed earn less [@levine_smart_2017]. In transition economies, own-account workers resemble the hidden unemployed, while employers resemble entrepreneurs [@earle_business_2000]. People who start businesses out of necessity also differ from those who start businesses to take up an opportunity, both in their characteristics and in their later earnings [@block_necessity_2010; @fairlie_2020]. A multinomial logit model of entry into each type of business would show whether the push we find, and its larger size for migrants with limited English, applies only to own-account work. Second, our sample treats a former owner who starts another business in the same way as a person starting their first business. Former owners have business experience, networks and a history of past success or failure, so their reasons for starting again may differ from those of first-time owners [@stam_renascent_2008]. Separating first entries from re-entries, and modelling the full sequence of entry, exit and re-entry, would show whether the push applies mainly to new owners and how long necessity entrants remain owners.

Finally, our study is based on Australia. Australian workplace law makes employers fully responsible for compliance, and it is enforced more actively than in many similar countries [@wright_2020]. The mechanism we study depends on strict compliance rules and on the presence of many migrant-owned businesses, and not on features unique to Australia. We therefore expect our findings to apply, at least in general terms, to other countries with many migrant-owned small businesses. Repeating our analysis with data from the United Kingdom, the United States or Canada, where enforcement differs, would show how much the strength of enforcement affects the position of migrant owners.
